title: Execution Prevention
summary: Execution prevention is the set of endpoint and policy controls that stop unauthorised code from ever running, rather than detecting it after it starts. In practice it is implemented as a layered stack: application allow-listing through Windows Defender Application Control or AppLocker, PowerShell constrained language mode and script block logging paired with a hardened execution policy, Microsoft Office macro restrictions enforced by group policy, and on Linux systems mount-level noexec flags plus integrity tooling. The control works because it denies the final common step of nearly every intrusion: the moment a payload is handed to a scripting host, a signed binary proxy, or an office application. It breaks behaviours such as user execution of a malicious attachment, abuse of command and scripting interpreters, and the broad family of living-off-the-land binary abuse where legitimate signed tools are repurposed to launch attacker code. Operational reality is unforgiving. Effective allow-listing requires months of audit-only telemetry, a disciplined change process for every legitimate software update, and a publisher-certificate strategy that survives vendor re-signing. Blocking PowerShell outright is rarely feasible; constrained language mode and AMSI integration are the practical compromise, and both are trivially weakened by an unmanaged host or an excluded directory. Common failure modes include allow-listing only the user-writable portions of the filesystem while leaving temporary and download directories executable, forgetting that signed interpreters such as mshta and rundll32 can load remote content, and deploying policy to workstations while leaving jump servers and build agents in audit mode indefinitely. Attackers adapt by moving to in-memory execution, signed binary proxy chains, and interpreter features that fall outside the constrained set, so execution prevention must be paired with memory-level detection and strict egress control to remain meaningful.
objectives: Explain how application allow-listing policies such as WDAC and AppLocker are designed, piloted in audit mode, and enforced without breaking business software.
Describe the practical difference between blocking a scripting interpreter outright and constraining its language mode, and when each is defensible.
Identify the signed binary proxy execution paths and interpreter features that most often bypass execution prevention controls.
Explain how Office macro, ActiveX, and add-in policy settings reduce user-execution risk and where they are commonly misconfigured.
Describe how noexec mounts, integrity verification, and package trust work on Linux and Unix endpoints as execution prevention.
Evaluate the operational cost of allow-listing in a changing environment and design a change-management path that keeps policy current.
Explain why execution prevention must be complemented by memory-level detection and egress control rather than treated as a complete control.
